intuition: A hash table turns a repeated search into a question you can answer from memory. Before choosing a map, finish this sentence: “For the current element, I need to know ___ about the elements already processed.” That blank determines what to store.

A set stores existence. A map can store a frequency, an index, or a group. The key must represent exactly the relationship you care about: the number itself for complement lookup, or a canonical signature for anagrams.
steps: Define the query
For a pair sum, the missing value is target − current. For grouping, the query is which bucket has the same signature.
Choose the stored value
Store an index to return positions, a count to count matches, or a list to collect all matching items.
Decide query versus update order
Query earlier elements before inserting the current element when using the same position twice is forbidden.
Explain what the map represents
After each iteration, it summarizes the processed prefix. Use this statement to justify that every reported match is legal.
patterns: Use a HashSet when the answer only depends on whether a value exists.
Use a count rather than a boolean when identical values represent multiple possible answers.
Convert equivalent objects to the same key, while ensuring nonequivalent objects stay separate.

examples.baseline: Checking every pair costs O(n²); most work repeats the same search for a complement.
reasoning: At index i, any earlier partner must equal target − nums[i]. A map from value to index answers that exact question.
If the complement is absent, record this value for later positions. Querying first also handles [3,3] with target 6 without ever pairing an element with itself.
codeNotes: seen.get(need) retrieves the partner index; i is the current index.
A repeated value may replace an older index because this task asks for any valid pair, not every pair.
examples.takeaway: The useful state is the earlier prefix, not a map of the entire input.

examples.baseline: Comparing each word with every existing group repeats character counting and can require quadratically many comparisons.
reasoning: Sort each word’s characters. Two words have the same sorted sequence exactly when their letter multiplicities match.
Use that sequence as a String key and append the original word, preserving its spelling. Group iteration order is irrelevant here.
codeNotes: computeIfAbsent creates a list only for a new key.
A char[] is converted to String because Java arrays do not provide content-based equals/hashCode by default.
examples.takeaway: The hard part of grouping is defining equality through the key.

1.optimization: For lowercase English words, a 26-count signature can avoid sorting each word. Encode counts with separators or a proper value object; concatenating bare counts can create ambiguous keys. Include the cost of constructing and hashing keys in the analysis.
pitfalls: Inserting too soon
A self-match can appear in Two Sum. Query before insertion.
Using existence when multiplicity matters
A set loses how many earlier matches exist; use counts for counting tasks.
Calling every lookup worst-case O(1)
State expected hash costs and account for the length of string keys.
1.interview: “The repeated work is searching the prefix. I will store each earlier value’s index, query the complement first, then insert. That gives expected linear time with linear extra memory.”
1.summary: Design the query first. Store precisely the information needed to answer it later.

intuition: Two pointers are useful when a proof lets you discard candidates without inspecting them one by one. On sorted input, a comparison can rule out every pair involving one endpoint.

The pointers do not always move toward each other. In compaction, a read pointer inspects input while a write pointer marks where the next accepted value belongs. What matters is the meaning of the regions they separate.
steps: Define the candidate region
For sorted pair search, possible partners remain between left and right.
Evaluate the endpoints
Compare their sum with the target using a type wide enough for arithmetic.
Prove a move is safe
If even the largest partner is too small for left, discard left. If even the smallest partner is too large for right, discard right.
Handle output identity
Returning indices, returning unique values, and modifying an array need different duplicate and boundary rules.
patterns: A sorted pair search eliminates one endpoint per failed comparison.
Move accepted values into a prefix without disturbing their relative order.
For 3Sum, choose a first value and use a pair search on the remaining suffix.

examples.baseline: A nested pair scan tries O(n²) candidates even though the input is already sorted.
reasoning: If numbers[left] + numbers[right] is too large, pairing right with any larger left index only increases the sum. No answer uses that right endpoint.
The symmetric argument applies to a sum that is too small. Each move removes only impossible pairs, so an existing answer stays in the interval.
codeNotes: left < right prevents using one position twice.
Casting before addition prevents overflow; adding 1 to each returned index follows this problem’s output contract.
examples.takeaway: Pointer movement follows from sorted order, not from the fact that there are two indices.

examples.baseline: Three nested loops enumerate O(n³) triples and still need a way to remove duplicate outputs.
reasoning: Sort first. For each fixed nums[i], search the suffix for a pair summing to −nums[i]. This reduces each fixed-value search to linear time.
Skip repeated fixed values. After a match, move both endpoints and skip their repeated values so each value triplet appears once.

trace.caption: 3Sum: sorted input [-4,-1,-1,0,1,2]
rows: Increase left; this fixed value has no answer

codeNotes: left starts at i + 1, so all three positions are different.
Sorting mutates nums; copy first if the caller needs its original order.
examples.takeaway: Deduplicate choices at the level where they are made.

2.optimization: If input is unsorted and original indices matter, a map may avoid sorting and index bookkeeping. In 3Sum, sorting costs O(n log n), but the repeated suffix scans dominate at O(n²). Report output space separately.
pitfalls: Moving pointers on unsorted values
Without an order guarantee, the elimination proof fails.
Mixing unique indices and unique values
Different index triples may represent the same 3Sum answer.
Forgetting the smallest inputs
Check two-element pair inputs and fewer than three elements for 3Sum.
2.interview: “I can eliminate this endpoint because even its best remaining partner cannot produce the target. Each pointer moves only forward through its range, giving a linear pair scan.”
2.summary: A pointer is a boundary between candidates still possible and candidates proved impossible.

intuition: A sliding window is a contiguous interval whose state can be updated as its endpoints move. Instead of rebuilding the sum or counts for every substring, add the entering item and remove the departing one.

Contiguity alone does not justify the technique. You also need a safe rule for abandoning a left endpoint. Uniqueness supports that rule; sums of positive numbers do too. Negative numbers can break the sum argument.
steps: Define window state
Write what [left,right] means and what counters or totals describe it.
Expand by one
Add input[right] before deciding whether the new window is valid.
Choose the shrink rule
For longest valid windows, shrink while invalid. For shortest valid windows, record candidates and shrink while valid.
Record at the right moment
Measure a longest window only after restoring validity; measure a shortest window before removing its left element.
Count total movement
Each endpoint advances at most n times, even though the code contains a nested loop.
patterns: Maintain exactly k elements and evaluate only once a full window exists.
Restore a constraint such as no duplicate characters, then maximize length.
While the window meets a requirement, minimize its length and try discarding the leftmost value.

examples.baseline: Checking every substring from scratch costs O(n³); even an incremental scan from every start repeats O(n²) work.
reasoning: The existing window is distinct before the next character arrives. Therefore only the newly added character can have a count above one.
Remove characters from the left until that duplicate disappears. The resulting window is the longest valid one ending at this right boundary.
codeNotes: The while loop may remove several characters; one removal is not necessarily enough.
Java char counts UTF-16 code units here. A user-perceived Unicode character may contain more than one unit.
examples.takeaway: Maintain validity before recording the longest answer.

examples.baseline: Enumerating every subarray costs O(n²) with running sums.
reasoning: Because all values are positive, extending right can only increase the sum and removing left can only decrease it.
For each right boundary, keep shortening every sufficient window. Once it becomes insufficient, further removal cannot help until right advances.
codeNotes: Update best before subtracting nums[left].
The sentinel n + 1 distinguishes “no valid window” from a real length; return 0 for the former.
examples.takeaway: Longest-valid and shortest-sufficient windows record answers on opposite sides of the shrink condition.

3.optimization: An array of counts can replace a map for a fixed small alphabet. A last-seen-index map can jump left for uniqueness, but left must never move backward. For exact sums with negative numbers, switch to prefix sums and a frequency map.
pitfalls: Using if instead of while
One removal may leave the window invalid.
Measuring before restoring validity
The recorded longest range might still contain duplicates.
Ignoring positivity
A negative value can make a formerly discarded start useful again in a sum problem.
3.interview: “My window state is updated on both entry and exit. I can discard these left endpoints because the constraint changes monotonically in this setting. Each element enters and leaves at most once.”
3.summary: Reuse the state of neighboring ranges, and prove why a discarded start will not be needed again.

intuition: A prefix total stores the answer from the beginning up to a boundary. Subtracting two such totals cancels their shared beginning and leaves only the interval between them.
Use boundaries rather than element indices: prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements. Then the half-open range [left,right) has sum prefix[right] − prefix[left], including when left is zero.
steps: Define the prefix precisely
Allocate n + 1 entries and let prefix[0] describe the empty prefix.
Translate the range equation
An exact sum k means currentPrefix − earlierPrefix = k, so the earlier value must be currentPrefix − k.
Choose what to remember
Store raw prefix totals for queries, counts for the number of ranges, or earliest indices for maximum length.
Seed the empty boundary
The initial zero is a real possible start boundary, not a special-case trick.
Query before recording
When counting nonempty ranges, insert the current prefix only after looking up earlier matches.
patterns: Preprocess once and answer each sum with a subtraction.
Find or count earlier boundaries with a required prefix value, even when values are negative.
When subtraction is unavailable, combine the contribution before and after each position.

examples.baseline: Try every start and end while maintaining a running sum: O(n²). A window based on sum comparisons does not work with arbitrary negatives.
reasoning: A subarray ending here has sum k exactly when its starting boundary has prefix value current − k.
Store how many times each earlier prefix occurred. Equal totals at different boundaries represent different ranges and must all count.

trace.caption: Count sum 2 in [1,1,1]; start with frequency {0:1}

codeNotes: The map key and running prefix use long to protect cumulative arithmetic.
For [0,0] and k=0, query-before-update yields 1 + 2 = 3 ranges, demonstrating why multiplicity matters.
examples.takeaway: Each stored prefix occurrence corresponds to one possible starting boundary.

examples.baseline: Summing each requested interval separately can take O(n) per query.
reasoning: Build prefix[i+1] by adding nums[i] to prefix[i]. A query uses two totals that share all values before left.
The public query uses an inclusive right index, so convert it to the exclusive boundary right + 1 before subtracting.
codeNotes: The extra array entry handles ranges beginning at zero uniformly.
NumArray is a named class: construct it once, then call sumRange repeatedly.
examples.takeaway: Be explicit about whether an index names an element or a boundary.

4.optimization: Prefix totals are excellent when the array stays unchanged. A single update can invalidate many later prefixes, so frequent updates need another structure. For Product of Array Except Self, store left products and sweep backward with a running right product; division is unnecessary and zeros are handled naturally.
pitfalls: Forgetting prefix zero
Ranges beginning at the first element disappear.
Storing only distinct prefix values
You lose distinct starts with equal totals.
Using prefix subtraction for minimum
Minimum has no inverse operation that removes the shared prefix.
4.interview: “I will express the range answer as a difference between two boundaries. For each current boundary, a map counts how many earlier boundaries have the required total.”
4.summary: Turn a range question into a relationship between two prefix boundaries.

intuition: Sorting pays an upfront cost to make a global relationship local. Equal keys become adjacent, interval starts become ordered, and a scan can decide when a result is complete.
The key question is not simply whether sorting is allowed. Ask what becomes provably easier after sorting, and whether you need to preserve the original positions or order.
steps: Choose the ordering
Identify the property that should become adjacent or monotone: starts, ends, values, or canonical signatures.
Define the scan summary
Track only what the processed region must tell the next item.
Prove when output is final
Use the sorted order to show that no later item can change a completed result.
Account for sorting
Include comparison cost, workspace, and input mutation in your explanation.
patterns: Ordering interval starts turns many overlap comparisons into a single forward scan.
Canonicalize an object, such as the letters of a word, to make equivalence easy to test.
Order objects according to the final objective; Largest Number compares a+b with b+a, not ordinary numeric order.

examples.baseline: Repeatedly comparing and merging arbitrary overlapping pairs can revisit intervals many times.
reasoning: Sort intervals by start. The next interval either extends the last merged interval or begins a new disjoint result.
If its start exceeds the last end, every later start does too. That proves the previous merged interval is finished.
codeNotes: Integer.compare avoids subtraction overflow in the comparator.
Cloning a newly appended interval prevents later end updates from changing that input interval’s contents, though the input array is still reordered.
examples.takeaway: Sorting supplies the proof that a completed interval will never need reopening.

examples.baseline: Pairwise anagram testing repeats work for the same words.
reasoning: Instead of sorting the whole input, sort the characters inside each word. That gives each equivalence class a single canonical representation.
A map then collects words by canonical key. Sorting and hashing solve different parts: defining equality and finding the group.
codeNotes: Keep the original s in the result, not the sorted key.
For n words of maximum length k, sorting happens n times on length-k data; it is not O(n log n).
examples.takeaway: Specify exactly what is sorted and what one comparison or key construction costs.

5.optimization: If keys come from a small fixed universe, counting can replace comparison sorting. If data is already sorted, preserve that advantage and skip the sort. When original indices must survive, sort value/index pairs or choose an approach that leaves the array intact.
pitfalls: Sorting by the wrong field
Merging uses starts; selecting the most compatible intervals uses ends.
Treating comparison as always O(1)
Comparing long strings or concatenated keys can inspect many characters.
Assuming sorting is free of side effects
Arrays.sort changes the passed array; document or avoid that mutation.
5.interview: “After ordering by this key, I can finalize each group when the key changes. I will justify the linear scan separately from the sorting cost and explain whether input order changes.”
5.summary: Sort to create a useful guarantee, then spend that guarantee in a simple scan.

intuition: Binary search repeatedly keeps the half that can still contain the answer. A sorted array is one way to get this property; the deeper requirement is a monotone decision that separates impossible positions from possible ones.

An exact search asks whether one value exists. A boundary search asks where a condition first becomes true. Duplicates make the distinction important: finding an arbitrary equal element does not locate the beginning of its block.
steps: Write the interval convention
Choose closed [left,right] or half-open [left,right). Do not mix their loop conditions or updates.
Define the decision
For lower bound, the condition is nums[mid] >= target. For exact search, equality can return immediately.
Remove a proven impossible region
Keep mid when it could be the boundary; discard it when it is known to fail.
Prove progress and termination
Each update must strictly shrink the candidate range. At exit, check whether a found boundary actually contains the target.
patterns: Return an index on equality or -1 after the candidate interval becomes empty.
Keep mid as the right boundary when it meets the condition.
Identify which half is sorted, then test whether the target falls in that half’s value range.

examples.baseline: A linear scan uses O(n) comparisons despite the sorted input.
reasoning: Keep a closed interval that contains the target if the target exists. If the middle value is too small, everything at or before it is too small.
Discard mid with mid + 1 or mid − 1. Equality is handled before discarding either half.
codeNotes: left <= right checks the final single candidate.
left + (right − left) / 2 avoids adding two potentially large indices.
examples.takeaway: The update rules are a consequence of the closed-interval invariant.

examples.baseline: A scan can find both ends in O(n), but the duplicate block has searchable boundaries.
reasoning: Find the first value >= target, then the first value > target. The target’s block is the half-open interval between those boundaries.
The first boundary may equal n or point to a different value. Reject those cases before indexing or returning a range.
codeNotes: right starts at nums.length because a boundary may lie after the final element.
A strict comparison flag avoids searching for target + 1, which could overflow.
examples.takeaway: Search for the boundary you need, rather than repairing an arbitrary match.

6.optimization: The O(log n) guarantee counts comparisons on random-access data. Repeatedly finding a midpoint in a linked list does not have the same cost. For rotated arrays with duplicates, equal endpoints can hide which half is sorted, and worst-case linear work may be necessary.
pitfalls: Combining incompatible templates
A half-open loop and closed-interval update can skip the answer.
Returning a boundary without validating it
The insertion point need not contain the target.
Keeping the same interval
Updates such as left = mid can stall with two candidates.
6.interview: “My interval contains every remaining candidate. This comparison rules out one half, and the update strictly shrinks the interval. For duplicates I will search two boundaries rather than one arbitrary occurrence.”
6.summary: Define the boundary and interval before writing the loop.

intuition: Sometimes checking a proposed answer is much easier than constructing the best answer directly. Binary search on the answer repeatedly asks whether a candidate limit is sufficient.

You need a proof of monotonicity. If speed k finishes all piles in time, every higher speed also does. The feasibility sequence is therefore false, false, …, true, true; the task is to find its first true value.
steps: Name the answer variable
Search a speed, capacity, or maximum permitted cost, rather than an array index.
Build a correct feasibility check
Decide whether one candidate can satisfy the original constraints, preserving order or other restrictions.
Prove monotonicity
Explain why increasing or decreasing the candidate cannot reverse feasibility in the wrong direction.
Choose valid bounds
Use a lower bound no answer can beat and an upper bound known to work.
Find the first feasible value
On success keep mid as a candidate; on failure discard mid and everything smaller.
patterns: Search the smallest speed or capacity that meets a deadline.
Check whether all work can be split while keeping each group below a candidate limit.
Reverse the predicate direction and use a last-true search with matching boundary rules.

examples.baseline: Trying every speed up to the largest pile costs O(nM).
reasoning: At speed k, each pile takes ceil(pile/k) hours because an hour cannot be shared between piles. Add these hours and compare with h.
Speed 1 is a lower bound. The largest pile is feasible when h is at least the number of piles. Higher speed never increases the required hours.
codeNotes: (pile + (long) mid − 1) / mid computes a ceiling using integer arithmetic.
hours is long because many individually small terms may have a large total.
examples.takeaway: Search correctness depends on both the monotone predicate and safe arithmetic.

examples.baseline: Testing every capacity between the largest weight and total weight repeats too many full scans.
reasoning: For a fixed capacity, load the longest next prefix that fits each day. Stopping a day earlier cannot reduce the number of remaining days for positive, ordered packages.
Increasing capacity cannot require more days. The largest weight is the lower bound; the total weight ships everything in one day.
codeNotes: The scan keeps package order; sorting weights would solve a different problem.
When a package does not fit, begin a new day and then add that same package.
examples.takeaway: Prove the checking algorithm before placing it inside binary search.

7.optimization: Stop a feasibility scan early once it has already exceeded the allowed hours or days. Total time is number of checks × work per check: typically O(n log R) for search-range size R, not merely O(log n).
pitfalls: Searching without monotonicity
A true/false/true feasibility pattern cannot be binary-searched this way.
Choosing an infeasible upper bound
The first-true search relies on an answer inside the interval.
Confusing at most and exactly
Finishing within d days allows fewer days; the predicate must match that wording.
7.interview: “I will first solve the yes/no version for a fixed capacity. Since any feasible capacity remains feasible when increased, I can binary-search the smallest one, paying a linear scan per check.”
7.summary: Turn optimization into a monotone decision problem.

intuition: Intervals describe coverage. Merging asks for the union of that coverage, while scheduling asks which intervals to keep. Similar pictures can therefore require different sorting rules and proofs.
Start with endpoint semantics. Closed [1,3] and [3,5] intersect at 3; half-open [1,3) and [3,5) do not. The comparison operator encodes this decision.
steps: State overlap semantics
Decide whether touching counts as intersection.
Exploit the available order
Sort by start unless the input already supplies sorted, disjoint intervals.
Maintain a current union
Extend its end with max(currentEnd,nextEnd), including nested intervals.
Finalize only after a gap
Once the next start is beyond the current end, later sorted starts cannot reconnect that union.
patterns: Sort starts and maintain the last output interval.
Copy intervals before the new one, merge overlaps, then copy those after it.
Use an earliest-finish greedy argument instead of merging coverage.

examples.baseline: Checking all pairs detects overlap but does not directly organize transitive chains of overlap.
reasoning: After sorting starts, compare each interval only with the last merged result. Earlier output intervals are already separated by a gap.
When overlap occurs, retain the smaller start already stored and take the larger end. A contained interval must never shorten the union.
codeNotes: The gap test uses lastEnd < nextStart; equality stays in the merge branch.
Math.max is necessary even though starts are sorted, because ends need not be.
examples.takeaway: Sorted starts do not imply sorted ends.

examples.baseline: Appending and sorting would work in O(n log n), but discards the input’s stronger guarantee.
reasoning: The existing intervals are already sorted and disjoint. They fall into three consecutive regions: strictly before, intersecting, and strictly after the new interval.
As overlaps extend the new end, more intervals can join the intersecting region. Use the updated end in the loop condition.
codeNotes: Local start and end variables avoid changing newInterval itself.
Untouched interval arrays are shared with the input; callers needing fully independent results should clone them.
examples.takeaway: Use an input guarantee to remove work, not just to simplify a proof.

8.optimization: Insertion is O(n) when order and disjointness are guaranteed. General merging is O(n log n) because of sorting. If only the count of simultaneous overlaps is needed, sweep events instead of constructing merged intervals.
pitfalls: Replacing rather than maximizing the end
A nested interval can accidentally shrink coverage.
Using one overlap rule everywhere
Scheduling may allow touching even when merging treats it as overlap.
Resorting guaranteed ordered input
Unnecessary sorting loses the linear insertion bound.
8.interview: “I will clarify whether endpoints overlap, then maintain the union of the current overlapping run. A gap proves that run is final because all future starts are larger.”
8.summary: Choose between coverage, compatibility, and concurrency before choosing the interval algorithm.

intuition: A sweep line represents changes instead of every position. An interval adds an amount at its start and removes it when it stops contributing. Scanning events in order reconstructs the active total.
This is a sparse prefix sum. A difference array stores events at every coordinate; an ordered map stores only coordinates where something changes. The endpoint convention decides when removal occurs.
steps: Define the active quantity
It may be passengers, overlapping intervals, or accumulated bookings.
Encode start and stop events
Add the contribution at the start and subtract it at the first coordinate where it no longer applies.
Combine equal coordinates
Make simultaneous changes follow the intended endpoint semantics.
Sweep in order
Accumulate deltas and check capacity or update the maximum active count.
patterns: For a trip from pickup to drop-off, remove passengers at drop-off before interpreting the onward segment.
For [l,r], add at l and remove at r+1; this requires discrete coordinates.
A bounded difference array turns each update into two writes followed by one prefix scan.

examples.baseline: Simulating every passenger at every position wastes work across long stretches with no changes.
reasoning: For [passengers,start,end], add passengers at start and subtract them at end. Riders leaving at x free seats for riders boarding at x.
A TreeMap combines all changes at each coordinate. Only the total on the segment after that coordinate needs a capacity check.
codeNotes: merge(position, delta, Integer::sum) handles multiple trips sharing a position.
The ordered map is essential; HashMap iteration would not follow the route.
examples.takeaway: The state describes the interval after an event coordinate.

examples.baseline: Trying assignments to groups can branch exponentially, although simultaneous overlap gives a direct lower bound.
reasoning: At any point with k active intervals, at least k groups are necessary. Processing starts in order and reusing any finished group also achieves this maximum overlap bound.
Because endpoints are closed integers, [1,3] is still active at 3. Remove its contribution at 4, not at 3.
codeNotes: Convert to long before computing end + 1.
This solution computes only the minimum count, not an actual assignment of interval IDs to groups.
examples.takeaway: A maximum-overlap lower bound is tight because ended groups can be reused.

9.optimization: Use an array when coordinates are small and dense, an ordered map when sparse, or sort an event list. An array costs O(n+U) for coordinate universe U; sorted sparse events cost O(n log n). Coordinate compression preserves order but not physical distances.
pitfalls: Removing a closed interval at its end
You miss overlap at a shared endpoint.
Checking halfway through equal-position changes
An artificial transient total can violate capacity even when the real state does not.
Allocating by the largest sparse coordinate
A few events should not require a billion-element array.
9.interview: “Only start and stop positions change the answer. I will encode their deltas, make equal-coordinate behavior explicit, and scan in order while maintaining the active total.”
9.summary: Store where the state changes, then recover the state by accumulation.

intuition: A linked-list problem is often a problem about preserving reachability while changing links. Unlike an array index, a next pointer may be the only reference you have to the unprocessed suffix.

Draw a processed region and an untouched region. Before assigning any next field, identify which node references would otherwise become unreachable. Dummy nodes simplify cases where the head itself changes.
steps: Name each pointer’s role
Use roles such as previous, current, next, and tail rather than treating pointers as interchangeable.
Save before rewiring
Preserve the next unprocessed node before changing current.next.
Maintain a region invariant
The processed prefix must already have the desired structure while the suffix remains reachable.
Handle the returned head
Return the new head or dummy.next, not whichever cursor happened to finish the loop.
patterns: Move one node at a time from the untouched suffix to the front of the reversed prefix.
Attach the smaller current head and advance only that list.
Deletion near the head becomes a normal predecessor-link update; a pointer gap locates a node from the end.

examples.baseline: Collecting node values and building a new reversed list costs O(n) extra space and creates different nodes.
reasoning: Let prev be the reversed prefix and current the first untouched node. Save current.next before redirecting current.next toward prev.
Advance prev to the node just processed and current to the saved suffix. When current is null, prev is the new head.
codeNotes: The order of the four assignments matters: save, redirect, advance prev, advance current.
An empty input skips the loop and returns null; a single node also works without a special case.
examples.takeaway: A saved reference is what makes destructive rewiring safe.

examples.baseline: Copying all values, sorting them, and rebuilding a list ignores both sorted inputs and costs extra storage.
reasoning: The smaller of the two current heads is the smallest remaining node overall. Attach it to tail and advance its source list.
Once one list ends, its partner’s suffix is already sorted and can be attached with one assignment.
codeNotes: The dummy node provides a stable predecessor for the first result node.
Reusing nodes changes the original links; this is not an independent copy of the lists.
examples.takeaway: Tail marks where the next proven-smallest node belongs.

10.optimization: Iterative reversal uses O(1) auxiliary space; a recursive version retains O(n) call frames. For two-pass list tasks, a pointer gap can sometimes remove the length pass, but only if the gap and null conditions are clearly defined.
pitfalls: Overwriting next too early
The remaining suffix may be lost.
Returning the moving cursor
At loop exit it is often null; return the saved head or prev.
Ignoring aliasing
Relinking shared input nodes affects every external reference to those nodes.
10.interview: “I will preserve the unprocessed suffix before each link update. At every step, this prefix is already correct and this pointer is the only boundary I need to advance.”
10.summary: Reason about reachable regions before reasoning about pointer assignments.

intuition: When repeatedly following a deterministic next link, the walk either ends or eventually revisits a node. Two cursors moving at different speeds can detect that repetition without storing every visited node.

The same speed ratio locates a midpoint in an acyclic list: when fast has traveled twice as far, slow has traveled about halfway. Cycle detection and midpoint search share a loop shape but have different stopping arguments.
steps: Define the walk
Identify one next transition: a list link or an array value interpreted as the next index.
Set the speeds
Advance slow once and fast twice per iteration.
Check before dereferencing
Both fast and fast.next must exist before taking two steps.
Interpret termination
Reaching null proves an acyclic walk; meeting after movement proves a cycle. For a midpoint, use where slow stops.
patterns: Compare node identity after moving; equal values alone are irrelevant.
Choose initialization and stopping rules according to first-middle or second-middle requirements.
An array can define a next-index function; Floyd’s method can then find a repeated-state cycle.

examples.baseline: A set of node identities detects repetition in O(n) time but needs O(n) memory.
reasoning: Once both pointers are in a cycle of length L, fast gains one position per iteration relative to slow. Their relative offset reaches zero within at most L iterations.
Compare references after advancing. Initially both are at head even in an acyclic list, so that initial equality does not prove a cycle.
codeNotes: slow == fast compares object identity, which is exactly the required repetition test.
The && guard short-circuits before fast.next is read when fast is null.
examples.takeaway: The proof is about relative movement within the cycle, not about values.

examples.baseline: Count nodes, then walk halfway: two linear passes and constant memory.
reasoning: After t iterations, slow has moved t links and fast has moved 2t links. One pass therefore gives the halfway position.
Starting both at head and stopping when fast or fast.next is null returns the second middle for even lengths.
codeNotes: The return value is a node, not its value.
This midpoint routine assumes the input list has no cycle; otherwise the loop never reaches null.
examples.takeaway: The even-length convention is determined by the loop, not by a final adjustment.

11.optimization: After a cycle meeting, resetting one cursor to head and moving both one step finds the cycle entrance. If the acyclic prefix has length μ and the cycle length is L, the meeting distance gives the modular relationship needed for the two cursors to meet at that entrance.
pitfalls: Comparing values
Two different nodes may contain the same number.
Checking equality before the first move
Both cursors start equal by construction.
Using midpoint logic on cyclic input
Its null-based termination argument no longer applies.
11.interview: “The fast pointer gains one step per iteration inside a cycle, so it must catch the slow pointer modulo the cycle length. If it reaches null first, the list is acyclic.”
11.summary: Different speeds reveal either a midpoint or repeated state; specify which conclusion the stopping condition supports.

intuition: A stack stores unfinished obligations in the order they must be resolved. The most recently opened bracket must close first; the most recently produced expression values become the next operands.
Use a stack when the next operation needs the latest unresolved item. This is a structural argument about nesting or evaluation order, not just a reason to choose a container with push and pop.
steps: Define one stack entry
It might be an expected closing bracket, a partial value, or a value paired with a running minimum.
Specify push and pop events
Describe which input creates unfinished work and which input resolves it.
Guard invalid operations
A required pop from an empty stack signals invalid input or a broken invariant.
Check the final state
Matching tasks require no outstanding obligations; expression evaluation requires the correct final value.
patterns: Store expected closing tokens and resolve the latest one first.
Store completed operands; an operator replaces its operands with their result.
Store a minimum with each depth so popping restores the previous minimum.

examples.baseline: Repeatedly deleting matching adjacent pairs can take O(n²) and obscures the nesting rule.
reasoning: When an opener arrives, push its expected closer. A closer is valid exactly when it equals the top outstanding obligation.
At the end, an empty stack means every opener was closed. Matching each encountered closer is insufficient if openers remain.

trace.caption: Bracket validation; stack shown bottom → top

codeNotes: Pushing expected closers avoids a separate opener-to-closer comparison during popping.
The solution assumes input contains only the six bracket characters.
examples.takeaway: The stack records what must happen next to remain valid.

examples.baseline: Building an expression tree and evaluating it works, but an explicit tree is unnecessary for postfix order.
reasoning: A number is already a completed expression. Push it. An operator consumes the latest two completed expressions and pushes one new result.
The first popped value is the right operand. Subtraction and division expose this order; addition and multiplication can conceal a bug.
codeNotes: Java integer division truncates toward zero, matching this problem.
Pop right first, then left, and evaluate left operator right.
examples.takeaway: Name operands explicitly instead of writing an order-sensitive expression with two pops.

12.optimization: ArrayDeque is a practical Java stack implementation. For Min Stack, pair every pushed value with the minimum at that depth, or maintain a second minimum stack with a consistent duplicate policy. O(1) minimum lookup requires preserving history across pops.
pitfalls: Reversing operands
right − left is wrong even though addition tests may pass.
Accepting leftover openers
A nonempty final stack means incomplete matching.
Dropping duplicate minima
Popping one copy must not erase the minimum represented by another copy.
12.interview: “Each entry is unfinished work. Because the newest obligation must be resolved first, a stack matches the dependency order. Every item is pushed and popped at most once.”
12.summary: A stack is a record of unresolved work whose resolution order is last-in, first-out.

intuition: A monotonic stack keeps unresolved candidates in sorted value order. A new value can settle several earlier questions at once, such as “when is the next warmer day?”
The inner pop loop is the useful work, not evidence of quadratic time. Once a candidate is resolved or dominated, it leaves permanently. Charging each pop to its earlier push gives a linear total.
steps: State the question per item
Decide whether you need the next greater, next smaller, or a boundary for a rectangle.
Choose what to store
Store indices when distance, position, or duplicate identity matters.
Define stack order and ties
Choose increasing or decreasing order and strict versus non-strict comparisons.
Resolve while the new item qualifies
Pop every candidate answered by the new value, then push the new unresolved item.
patterns: A decreasing stack waits for a larger incoming value.
Reverse the inequality and maintain increasing candidates.
A popped histogram bar uses its next smaller position and the remaining stack to determine its maximal width.

examples.baseline: Scanning forward from every day for a warmer temperature costs O(n²) in a descending sequence.
reasoning: Keep indices of days with no warmer day yet. Their temperatures are nonincreasing from bottom to top.
When a warmer day arrives, it is the first warmer day for each popped index: any earlier qualifying day would already have popped that index.
codeNotes: Use i − previous for the waiting time, not a difference of temperatures.
Unresolved entries keep the zero initialized in the answer array.
examples.takeaway: “Unresolved” gives each stack entry a reason to stay.

examples.baseline: For each query value, locate it and scan right again, repeating the same comparisons.
reasoning: Preprocess nums2 once with a decreasing stack. When x arrives, it is the next greater value for every smaller stack top it removes.
The problem guarantees distinct values in nums2, so a map keyed by value is sufficient. With duplicates and position-specific answers, store indices instead.
codeNotes: getOrDefault supplies -1 for values with no greater successor.
The map separates preprocessing from answering many queries.
examples.takeaway: Exploit distinctness only when the problem explicitly guarantees it.

13.optimization: For n inputs there are at most n pushes and n pops, yielding O(n) work despite nested loops. Circular next-greater tasks often scan the sequence twice while limiting which indices are initially pushed. Histogram tasks need a final flush or sentinel to resolve remaining bars.
pitfalls: Using the wrong equality rule
Equal temperatures are not warmer; use a strict greater comparison.
Storing only values for distances
Distances require positions.
Forgetting unresolved entries
They need the problem’s no-answer value or a final boundary flush.
13.interview: “The stack contains unresolved candidates in monotone order. The new item resolves a suffix of them permanently, so the total number of removals is linear.”
13.summary: Keep candidates until the first event that proves their answer, then remove them forever.

intuition: A monotonic deque is a queue of candidates that can still become a window’s best value. It removes expired indices from the front and dominated candidates from the back.

If a newer value is at least as large as an older one, the older one can never be a future maximum while both are eligible: it is no larger and it expires sooner. That dominance argument is why removal is permanent.
steps: Define eligibility
An index must remain inside the current window.
Expire from the front
Remove indices left behind by the moving window boundary.
Prune from the back
For a maximum, discard older values no greater than the new value.
Read the front
After updates, the front is the best eligible candidate.
Coordinate multiple deques if needed
A maximum and minimum deque together can enforce a range-spread constraint.
patterns: Use decreasing values and increasing indices.
Maintain both maximum and minimum while shrinking until their difference is allowed.
For shortest sum-at-least-K with negatives, a deque orders prefix totals rather than raw array values.

examples.baseline: Scanning k values for each window costs O(nk).
reasoning: Indices increase from front to back, so expired entries are found at the front. Values decrease, so the maximum is also at the front.
Before appending a new index, remove smaller or equal older values from the back. A newer equal value is preferable because it survives longer.
codeNotes: An index <= i − k lies outside the current window.
Output starts at i = k − 1, after the first complete window exists.
examples.takeaway: Expiration and domination are different reasons to remove an index.

examples.baseline: Checking every subarray’s maximum and minimum repeats work and can cost at least O(n²).
reasoning: A window satisfies all pairwise difference limits exactly when max − min <= limit. Two monotonic deques provide those extremes.
If adding a value breaks the condition, advance left and expire its indices until the condition is restored. Removing values cannot increase the spread.
codeNotes: Cast before subtracting minimum from maximum so a large spread cannot overflow.
Expire an index only from deque fronts that actually contain it. Dominated indices may already be absent.
examples.takeaway: A window can be summarized by extremes even when its condition mentions every pair.

14.optimization: Each index enters and leaves each deque at most once. Fixed-window maximum uses O(k) auxiliary space; a variable window may retain O(n) candidates. A heap offers general priority selection but does not automatically remove stale entries or give the same linear bound.
pitfalls: Storing no indices
Equal values cannot tell you which occurrence expired.
Removing from the wrong end
Expiration follows age; domination follows value.
Assuming contiguity alone permits a deque
You need a dominance proof showing removed candidates never become useful again.
14.interview: “A newer candidate with a better value dominates this older one because it also expires later. The front remains the best active candidate, and every index is processed only a constant number of times.”
14.summary: Keep only candidates that are both eligible now and capable of winning later.

intuition: Recursive tree code becomes easier when every call has a precise return contract. Ask what information a parent needs from one child, and define that before writing the recursion.

The value returned upward may differ from the final answer. A diameter can use two child branches through a node, but a path extended by the parent can use only one of those branches. Mixing these roles causes subtle mistakes.
steps: Define the return value
For height, return the number of nodes on the longest downward path starting here.
Set the empty-tree base case
A null subtree has height zero, so a leaf naturally has height one.
Solve children under that contract
Treat recursive results as correct summaries, rather than tracing every call at once.
Combine and update
Compute the value returned to the parent and separately update any best answer that may pass through this node.
patterns: Compute child results before combining height, balance, or subtree totals.
Pass constraints or path state downward when children need context.
A local path may join both children while the returned path can extend only one side.

examples.baseline: Recomputing each node’s depth by repeatedly finding paths from the root duplicates traversal work.
reasoning: The deepest root-to-leaf path must enter either the left or right subtree. Its length is one plus the larger child height.
Inductively, if each child returns its correct height, that formula returns the correct height here. Null returns zero to close the recursion.

trace.caption: Tree 3 with children 9 and 20; 20 has children 15 and 7

codeNotes: Each node is visited once; the recursion does not rescan subtrees.
Space is the maximum active call depth h, not the total n calls made over time.
examples.takeaway: A one-sentence return contract can serve as the induction hypothesis.

examples.baseline: Computing subtree heights from scratch at every possible path center can take O(n²) on a chain.
reasoning: At a node with child heights left and right, the longest path passing through it has left + right edges.
Return only 1 + max(left,right) upward. Returning both branches would create a fork when a parent tries to extend that path.
codeNotes: The diameter field stores the best path anywhere, including paths that do not cross the root.
Reset diameter for each public call so reusing the Solution object is safe.
examples.takeaway: The parent needs an extendable summary; the overall answer may combine more information.

15.optimization: Both examples are O(n) time and O(h) stack space. Balanced trees have logarithmic height, but skewed trees can have linear height and overflow Java’s recursion stack. An explicit stack can simulate postorder when depth is unbounded.
pitfalls: Counting nodes when edges are requested
Diameter uses left + right, while height returns one extra node.
Returning a forked path
A parent cannot extend two child branches as one simple path.
Assuming all trees are balanced
Worst-case stack depth is n.
15.interview: “My helper returns the subtree height. After obtaining both child heights, I update the best path through this node and return only the longer downward branch for its parent.”
15.summary: Define what flows upward, and separate it from what is recorded as the final answer.

intuition: Breadth-first traversal processes a tree by distance from the root. A queue holds discovered nodes waiting for their turn, with earlier levels ahead of later ones.
To produce separate levels, capture the queue size before processing a layer. Children added during that layer belong to the next one; using a changing queue size would blur those boundaries.
steps: Handle the empty root
Return the empty result before trying to enqueue null.
Queue the initial level
Start with the root as the only depth-zero node.
Freeze the layer size
Process exactly the number of nodes present at the start of the layer.
Collect and expand
Record the information needed from this layer, then enqueue nonnull children in a consistent order.
patterns: Collect every value from a layer into a separate list.
Take the first or last node according to enqueue order.
For minimum depth, the first leaf encountered by BFS gives the shortest root-to-leaf path.

examples.baseline: A DFS can collect nodes by depth, but must explicitly carry depth and manage the corresponding output lists.
reasoning: The queue already encodes the depth ordering. Capture size, remove exactly that many nodes, and place their values in one result list.
Enqueue left before right so the next layer appears in the usual left-to-right order.
codeNotes: size is a snapshot, not queue.size() reevaluated on every for-loop condition.
The output contains all n values, while the queue needs space proportional to maximum width.
examples.takeaway: A queue-size snapshot separates the current frontier from the next.

examples.baseline: Rendering coordinates or comparing every node’s position is unnecessary for the right side view.
reasoning: With children queued left before right, the last node removed from a level is its rightmost visible node.
A deeper visible node need not lie on a chain of right children. A left subtree can extend below the right subtree and become visible there.
codeNotes: i == size − 1 selects the last node in this fixed layer.
Changing child enqueue order requires changing which position is selected.
examples.takeaway: Visibility follows layer order, not simply repeated right-child selection.

16.optimization: BFS uses O(w) auxiliary memory for maximum width w; DFS uses O(h) active stack depth. Choose based on the needed information and possible tree shape. An early-return minimum-depth BFS can avoid exploring deeper layers after finding a leaf.
pitfalls: Using the growing queue size
New children may be processed as if they were on the current level.
Enqueuing null into ArrayDeque
It does not allow null elements; guard each child.
Calling every missing child a leaf
A leaf has neither child; one missing child does not terminate a root-to-leaf path.
16.interview: “The queue starts each iteration with exactly one level. I will process a fixed number of nodes, collect the required information, and leave all their children for the next iteration.”
16.summary: Treat a level as a frozen frontier, then build the next frontier behind it.

intuition: A binary search tree imposes constraints on entire subtrees, not just direct children. Every node in a left subtree must be smaller than its ancestor, and every node in a right subtree must be larger under the strict convention used here.
That global order provides two useful views: each descent narrows an allowed value interval, and inorder traversal emits values in sorted order. Pick the view that matches the question.
steps: Clarify the duplicate rule
These problems use strict ordering; duplicates violate it.
Choose bounds or inorder
Bounds prove validity; inorder supports ordered enumeration and rank.
Carry inherited constraints
A child must obey all ancestor restrictions, not just compare with its parent.
Stop when the requested information is known
A rank query can finish after visiting k inorder nodes, though reaching them may require descending h levels.
patterns: Each node belongs to an open interval inherited from ancestors.
Traverse left, node, right and count visited nodes.
For BST lowest common ancestor, descend while both targets lie strictly on the same side.

examples.baseline: Checking only node.left < node < node.right misses violations deeper inside a subtree.
reasoning: Pass an exclusive lower and upper bound. A left descent replaces the upper bound with the current value; a right descent replaces the lower bound.
Use long bounds around int node values so the smallest and largest int remain legal values.
codeNotes: <= low and >= high reject duplicates as well as out-of-range nodes.
Null subtrees are valid; they contain no counterexample to the constraints.
examples.takeaway: Inherited bounds express all ancestor requirements in constant-size state.

examples.baseline: Collecting and sorting all tree values discards BST ordering and always visits every node.
reasoning: Simulate inorder traversal using a stack. Descend left to reach the smallest unvisited node, then pop and count it.
After visiting a node, its right subtree contains the next larger candidates. Stop when the kth visit occurs.
codeNotes: The inner loop saves ancestors that must be revisited after their left subtree.
This example uses k=2 to show the transition from one node into its right subtree.
examples.takeaway: Inorder traversal is an ordered iterator, so a rank query can stop early.

17.optimization: A BST is not necessarily balanced: h can be n. Repeated rank queries can benefit from stored subtree sizes, but those sizes must be maintained after updates. For a single query, an inorder stack avoids changing the tree.
pitfalls: Checking only parent-child pairs
A descendant can violate a more distant ancestor.
Using int extrema as exclusive sentinels
Legal endpoint int values would be rejected.
Claiming O(log n) for every BST
That bound needs a height guarantee such as balancing.
17.interview: “Every recursive call receives the range allowed by its ancestors. For a rank query, inorder provides sorted order, so I can count visits without sorting the values again.”
17.summary: Use the ordering of whole subtrees, not just the shape of the tree.

intuition: Graph traversal explores connections while preventing repeated work. A grid is a graph whose vertices are cells and whose edges are the allowed moves; row and column coordinates replace an explicit adjacency list.

Choose the traversal by the required result. DFS or BFS can mark a connected component. BFS also supplies shortest distances when every edge has equal cost, and multiple starting points can share one initial frontier.
steps: Define vertices and edges
State whether movement is four-directional, diagonal, directed, or undirected.
Mark on discovery
Claim a node before recursively entering it or enqueuing it, so other paths do not schedule it again.
Choose the frontier
A stack explores deeply; a queue explores by distance.
Restart or seed as needed
Restart from every unvisited node to count components, or enqueue all initial sources to model simultaneous spread.
patterns: Every new traversal from unvisited land discovers one whole island.
BFS layers correspond to numbers of edges.
All initial sources have distance zero and expand together.

examples.baseline: Starting a fresh search from every land cell without shared visited state recounts the same island.
reasoning: Scan all cells. When unvisited land appears, increment the count once and flood its entire component.
Changing visited land to water prevents later scans from recounting it. This saves a separate visited array but mutates the input.
codeNotes: The flood guard rejects out-of-bounds coordinates and non-land before accessing neighbors.
Diagonal contact alone does not join (1,1) and (2,2) in this problem.
examples.takeaway: One increment belongs to one traversal start, not to every discovered cell.

examples.baseline: Simulating each rotten source separately repeats propagation and requires reconciling arrival times.
reasoning: Enqueue all initially rotten cells at minute zero. Each BFS layer is the set of cells that can infect neighbors during the next minute.
Mark a fresh cell rotten as soon as it is enqueued and decrement fresh once. If the frontier empties while fresh remains, those cells are unreachable.
codeNotes: The fresh > 0 loop guard prevents adding an extra minute after the last infection.
Multiple starting sources are all inserted before any propagation begins.
examples.takeaway: Simultaneous processes often become a single BFS with multiple sources.

18.optimization: Adjacency-list traversal costs O(V+E); a four-neighbor grid has O(RC) edges and costs O(RC). Matrix input may require O(V²) scanning. Recursive flood fill can use O(RC) call depth in the worst case, so use an explicit stack or queue for large grids.
pitfalls: Marking only when dequeued
The same node may be enqueued through several parents.
Ignoring input mutation
Flooding by overwriting cells destroys the original grid.
Using DFS depth as shortest distance
The first DFS path need not be the shortest one.
18.interview: “I will mark each cell when discovered, so it enters the frontier once. For spread time I need BFS layers, seeded with every source, and a count of cells that remain unreachable.”
18.summary: The visited rule controls repeated work; the frontier order controls what discovery tells you.

intuition: Topological order schedules directed dependencies. A node becomes available when every prerequisite has been processed. Its indegree is the number of incoming dependency edges still waiting to be removed.
A directed cycle has no first available node within the cycle. Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly processes zero-indegree nodes; if any nodes remain afterward, some dependency cycle prevents completion.
steps: Orient each edge
For “a requires b,” draw b → a so processing b can unlock a.
Count all indegrees
Include isolated vertices even when they appear in no edge.
Queue every available node
All indegree-zero nodes can be processed now; several choices may be valid.
Remove outgoing dependencies
Decrement each neighbor’s indegree once per processed edge and enqueue it when the count reaches zero.
Check completeness
An order is valid only if it includes every vertex.
patterns: Count processed vertices to decide whether all tasks can finish.
Record each removed vertex in sequence.
For eventual-safe states, reverse edges and remove nodes whose original outgoing choices are all safe.

examples.baseline: Trying every possible course ordering can require factorial work.
reasoning: Indegree counts unmet prerequisites. A zero count makes a course safe to complete immediately.
After removing every currently available course, either all courses are complete or the remaining subgraph has no zero-indegree vertex, implying a directed cycle.
codeNotes: graph.get(edge[1]).add(edge[0]) encodes prerequisite → dependent.
A processed count smaller than numCourses catches cycles even when another component was completed successfully.
examples.takeaway: Processing an acyclic component is not enough; every course must be included.

examples.baseline: Checking permutations for prerequisite violations does not exploit local availability.
reasoning: Use the same removal process but append each available course to an output array.
When two courses become available together, either order can be correct. The result needs to satisfy dependencies, not match one unique sequence.
codeNotes: Only enqueue a neighbor when its indegree becomes exactly zero.
If the output has fewer than numCourses entries, return an empty array rather than a partial schedule.
examples.takeaway: An availability queue produces one valid order, not necessarily the only one.

19.optimization: Every vertex and edge is handled once, for O(V+E). A DFS alternative uses unvisited, visiting, and finished states; an edge to a visiting node proves a cycle. A priority queue can choose the smallest available ID when a specific tie-breaking order is required, at additional cost.
pitfalls: Reversing the input pair
The produced order may violate every intended prerequisite.
Using ordinary visited flags to detect directed cycles
Revisiting a finished node is harmless; revisiting an active recursion node is not.
Forgetting isolated vertices
They are valid zero-indegree tasks and belong in the output.
19.interview: “Indegree will represent remaining prerequisites. I will repeatedly complete available tasks and remove their outgoing dependencies. A short output proves some tasks are trapped behind a cycle.”
19.summary: A topological order is a sequence of tasks that become available as dependencies disappear.

intuition: Union-find maintains groups as connections are added. Each group has a representative root, and two elements are connected exactly when their representatives match.

It stores connectivity, not the actual route connecting two nodes. That distinction makes it compact and fast for merges, but unsuitable by itself for path reconstruction, directed reachability, or ordinary edge deletion.
steps: Initialize singleton groups
Every element starts as its own parent with size one.
Find representatives
Follow parent links to roots; shorten the path along the way.
Merge roots only
If roots differ, attach the smaller tree beneath the larger and update its size.
Interpret repeated connections
Equal roots mean the new edge connects already-connected vertices; it does not reduce the number of components.
patterns: An edge whose endpoints are already connected closes a cycle.
Start at n groups and subtract one for every successful union.
Answer queries as edges are added, without rerunning a full traversal each time.

examples.baseline: For each incoming edge, run a traversal to see whether its endpoints are already connected; repeated searches can become quadratic.
reasoning: Maintain the components formed by earlier edges. If the next edge joins two different roots, merge them.
If the roots already match, an earlier path connects the endpoints. The new edge plus that path forms a cycle.
codeNotes: union returns false precisely when no merge occurs.
There are edges.length nodes with labels starting at 1 in this problem, so the arrays include one extra slot.
examples.takeaway: A failed merge can be the information the problem asks for.

examples.baseline: A graph traversal is already a good alternative; DSU offers a different way to accumulate the same connectivity from matrix entries.
reasoning: Begin with one component per city. For each connection above the matrix diagonal, attempt a union.
Only a successful union reduces the count. A redundant connection within one province must not decrement it again.
codeNotes: j starts at i + 1 because the matrix is symmetric and self-connections add no information.
The matrix still takes quadratic time to inspect even though DSU operations are very cheap.
examples.takeaway: Choose a method based on input representation as well as abstract graph size.

20.optimization: Path compression plus union by size gives O(α(n)) amortized time per operation, where α grows extremely slowly. Include O(n) initialization and any input scan. Ordinary DSU cannot split components after an edge deletion; that needs a different or more specialized technique.
pitfalls: Linking arbitrary nodes rather than roots
You can corrupt component structure or invalidate size accounting.
Reducing count on every edge
Only a successful merge changes the number of components.
Using DSU for directed dependencies
Mutual group membership does not capture directed reachability or ordering.
20.interview: “I only need to know which vertices are connected, so I will maintain representative roots. Each successful union merges two components; a repeated connection can reveal an undirected cycle.”
20.summary: Remember which group each node belongs to, not how the graph reaches it.

intuition: BFS finalizes nodes in edge-count order. When edges have unequal nonnegative costs, a priority queue instead selects the smallest tentative distance. This is Dijkstra’s central change: expand the best known unfinished path first.

A tentative distance is a candidate, not a promise. A node can be discovered through an expensive route and improved later. It becomes safe to expand when its current best entry is the smallest one removed from the heap.
steps: Define the path cost
For ordinary shortest paths, add edge weights. For bottleneck paths, take the maximum edge so far.
Initialize tentative labels
Set the source to zero and all other distances to infinity.
Extract the current best
Ignore heap entries whose stored distance no longer matches the best known label.
Relax outgoing edges
If extending the current path improves a neighbor, store the improvement and add a new heap entry.
Read the requested result
Return a target distance, the largest reachable distance, or failure if required nodes remain unreachable.
patterns: candidate = max(effort[u], edgeDifference); extension cannot improve an already accumulated bottleneck.
Use the best probability first; multiplying by probabilities in [0,1] cannot improve a path as it extends.

examples.baseline: Repeatedly relaxing every edge, as in Bellman–Ford, can take O(VE); nonnegative weights permit a more selective order.
reasoning: The heap gives the smallest current distance. A path through any farther unsettled node cannot become cheaper by adding nonnegative edges.
Relax each outgoing edge, allowing later improvements. Once all work finishes, the last arrival time is the maximum shortest distance from the source.
codeNotes: Heap ties may process nodes 1 and 3 in either order without changing the result.
The stale-entry check avoids re-expanding a node using an outdated, more expensive distance.
examples.takeaway: Discovery is provisional; the best current extraction supplies the greedy guarantee.

examples.baseline: Enumerating all simple grid paths is exponential and compares many paths with the same endpoint.
reasoning: The cost of a path is its largest height jump, not the sum of jumps. Extending a path updates its cost with max.
For a fixed endpoint, a smaller bottleneck is always at least as useful for every future extension. That dominance property makes one best label per cell sufficient.
codeNotes: The table traces an optimal path, not every heap extraction.
Return when the destination is removed with its current best effort; merely inserting it is too early.
examples.takeaway: The heap strategy can survive a changed path metric when its monotonicity proof survives too.

21.optimization: Lazy duplicate entries avoid needing a decrease-key operation. They use up to O(E) heap entries, giving O(V + E log(E+1)) time for the additive implementation. For equal-cost edges use BFS; negative edges invalidate the ordinary Dijkstra proof.
pitfalls: Marking final on insertion
A better path may arrive later.
Using sum for a bottleneck objective
That optimizes a different quantity.
Ignoring unreachable nodes
An infinity label must produce the specified failure result, not overflow an output cast.
21.interview: “The path cost cannot decrease when extended, so the smallest tentative label is safe to expand. I will relax neighbors and discard stale heap entries rather than finalizing a node when first discovered.”
21.summary: A best-first traversal needs a proof that an unfinished route cannot undercut the current best extraction.

intuition: A heap keeps one extreme cheap to access without fully sorting all elements. The root is the best or worst item under your comparator; the remaining array is only partially ordered.
Choose what the root should mean before choosing min-heap or max-heap. Keeping the k largest items often needs a min-heap, because the smallest retained item is the one you want to evict.
steps: Define the candidate set
Decide which items must compete right now: retained winners, list frontiers, or one half of a stream.
Choose the root’s role
It may be the next output item or the weakest item worth retaining.
Update and rebalance
Insert the incoming candidate, then remove or move an item to restore the invariant.
Analyze heap size
The logarithmic factor depends on the number of active heap entries, not automatically the total input size.
patterns: Keep at most k winners with their weakest at the root.
Keep one head from each unfinished source; after outputting it, add its successor.
Balance a max-heap of the lower half and min-heap of the upper half.

examples.baseline: Counting frequencies then fully sorting all unique values costs O(n + u log u) expected time.
reasoning: First count each value’s frequency. Keep a min-heap ordered by frequency and remove its smallest member whenever size exceeds k.
After each insertion, every discarded value is no more frequent than the retained candidates at that moment. The final heap contains k top-frequency values.

trace.caption: Frequencies for [1,1,1,2,2,3], k=2; illustrative key order 1,2,3

codeNotes: HashMap iteration order may differ; correctness does not depend on the illustrative order.
Frequencies are computed before heap insertion, so comparator priorities stay stable while values are inside the heap.
examples.takeaway: For Top K, put the weakest retained candidate at the root.

examples.baseline: Scanning every list head to choose each next node costs O(Nk).
reasoning: Only the current head of each sorted list can be its next output candidate. Put these heads in a min-heap.
Remove the smallest head, append that node, and add its successor. The heap again represents exactly the next candidate from each active list.
codeNotes: The heap holds at most k nodes even though the result has N nodes.
Input nodes are relinked; the result is not a separate copy. Equal-value nodes may be emitted in either source order.
examples.takeaway: Sorted sources let you represent many unseen items with one frontier each.

22.optimization: Frequency buckets can solve Top K in expected O(n) time when counts lie between 1 and n. Pairwise merging can match O(N log k) for sorted lists. A heap iterator is not sorted; repeatedly poll when sorted extraction is required.
pitfalls: Choosing the wrong root
A max-heap of all values does not provide the same bounded-memory Top K approach.
Changing priorities in place
Java PriorityQueue does not automatically reorder when a stored object’s comparator fields change.
Assuming iteration is sorted
Only the root and repeated removals have the promised ordering.
22.interview: “I only need repeated access to one extreme. I will keep this bounded candidate set in the heap, define what its root means, and count O(log k) work for each update.”
22.summary: Keep just enough candidates to identify the next winner or the next item to evict.

intuition: Backtracking explores a tree of partial decisions. At each level, choose a legal next action, explore everything that follows, then undo the action so a sibling branch starts from the same state.
The question determines whether order matters. A subset can be built using increasing input indices; a permutation must reconsider all unused positions because different orders are different answers.
steps: Define one recursive state
Describe the chosen path and which choices remain legal.
Decide when to record
Every path is a subset, while only full-length paths are complete permutations.
Enumerate legal choices
Use a start index, a used array, or problem-specific constraints.
Choose, recurse, undo
Restore every mutable field changed for the branch.
Copy saved answers
The working path is reused; a stored answer needs independent contents.
patterns: Increasing indices avoid generating the same selection in different orders.
Track used positions and allow every unused value at each depth.
Prune impossible partial choices early, such as revisiting a cell in one Word Search path.

examples.baseline: A bitmask can enumerate all subsets; recursive construction offers a more direct way to extend partial choices and later add constraints.
reasoning: Record the current path at every call, including the empty path. Then choose each possible next index at or after start.
Recurse with i + 1, ensuring indices increase. Each subset has exactly one increasing-index representation, so there are no duplicate construction paths.
codeNotes: new ArrayList<>(path) freezes the current contents for the result.
Removing the last element restores the path before the next loop choice.
examples.takeaway: A canonical construction order prevents duplicates before they are generated.

examples.baseline: Generating length-n sequences with repetition and filtering them afterward explores many illegal candidates.
reasoning: A used array prevents choosing the same input position twice. Every unused position remains available, regardless of its numeric index.
Only save when the path has n values. Restore both the path and used[i] when returning from a branch.

trace.caption: Permutations of [1,2,3]: beginning of the search

codeNotes: A start index would incorrectly forbid orders such as [2,1,3].
This code assumes distinct input values; duplicates require additional deduplication rules.
examples.takeaway: Order-sensitive output needs a different choice model from combinations.

23.optimization: Pruning helps only when rejected partial paths cannot lead to answers. Enumeration still pays for output: subsets require Θ(n·2^n) total element copying and permutations Θ(n·n!). If the task asks only for a count or optimum, repeated states may be merged with DP instead of listing paths.
pitfalls: Saving the live path
Every result may appear to change as recursion continues.
Undoing only some state
A leftover used flag can silently suppress valid sibling branches.
Calling exponential time a coding failure
Exponential-size output itself requires exponential work.
23.interview: “My path is a partial answer. I will enumerate each legal next choice once, restore state after exploring it, and copy completed results. Complexity includes the number and size of outputs.”
23.summary: Explore a decision, learn everything below it, then restore exactly the state you started from.

intuition: Dynamic programming stores answers to subproblems whose results are reused. Start with the question a recursive call would answer, then identify which calls ask that same question again. A cache can merge that repeated work.

A state is a promise about meaning: “dp[i] is the number of ways to reach stair i” differs from “reachable[i] says whether the first i characters can be segmented.” The table’s type, base cases, and transitions follow from that sentence—not the other way around.

Top-down memoization starts at the requested state and caches recursive results. Bottom-up tabulation computes states in dependency order. Both solve the same recurrence; neither guarantees polynomial time unless the number of states and work per state are suitably bounded.
steps: Define the state in one sentence
Say exactly which input prefix or suffix is represented and whether its answer is a count, a boolean, or an optimum.
Derive the final choice
Partition valid solutions by the last step, last word, or last action. This explains why the recurrence includes all legal possibilities.
Answer the smallest states directly
An empty prefix is segmentable; there is one empty way to reach stair zero. These are semantic base cases.
Choose dependency order
If state i needs earlier prefixes, fill left to right. A recursive solution reaches those dependencies through calls and caches them.
Locate the answer and then compress
The final answer may be dp[n], a maximum over entries, or a particular inventory state. Remove old entries only after proving they will not be read again.
patterns: Add disjoint alternatives, as in Climbing Stairs.
Use OR across possible previous states, as in Word Break.
Use min/max over choices; include extra state such as holding a stock when it changes future legal actions.

examples.baseline: Try every possible first word recursively. Different word choices can reach the same remaining suffix, causing repeated subproblems.
reasoning: Define reachable[end] as whether s[0:end] can be segmented. A final word s[start:end] succeeds when reachable[start] is true and the word is in the dictionary.
The empty prefix is reachable. Fill end from left to right so all smaller start boundaries are ready. Trying every legal last word preserves alternatives that greedy segmentation would discard.

trace.caption: Word Break: aaaaaaa with {aaa,aaaa}
rows: Neither 1 + aaaa nor 2 + aaa is reachable

codeNotes: maxLength limits candidate substrings to lengths present in the dictionary.
Java substring construction and hashing cost time proportional to substring length; counting boundary pairs alone understates the implementation cost.
examples.takeaway: A boolean state can preserve multiple valid histories without remembering every segmentation.

examples.baseline: Recursive ways(n−1) + ways(n−2) repeats the same stair counts in many branches.
reasoning: Define ways[i] as the number of ordered step sequences reaching stair i. Every path arrives from i−1 with a one-step move or i−2 with a two-step move; those cases are disjoint.
Use ways[0]=1 and ways[1]=1. A full table computes earlier entries once; the shown implementation keeps only the previous two because no future transition needs anything older.
codeNotes: At the start of iteration i, previous is ways[i−2] and current is ways[i−1].
Compute next before shifting variables so neither needed old value is overwritten.
examples.takeaway: Space optimization is a dependency-lifetime argument, not a different recurrence.

24.optimization: Memoization needs an “unknown” state distinct from a computed false or zero; Boolean[] with null can represent boolean memo states. Bottom-up removes recursion depth but may compute states a top-down search never reaches. House Robber compresses two previous optima; stock-with-fee needs separate cash and hold states using the previous day’s values.
pitfalls: Choosing an unclear state
“Best so far” is insufficient unless it specifies the processed input and retained constraints.
Treating every min/max problem as DP
First establish repeated subproblems and sufficient state; greedy or graph search may be better.
Compressing before deriving dependencies
Word Break can need many earlier prefixes, so two rolling variables are not a general 1D-DP rule.
24.interview: “I will define the subproblem, derive its final-choice cases, and state the base cases. Then I will cache repeated states or fill them in dependency order, count transitions, and only afterward consider memory compression.”
