24.summary: The recurrence is the reasoning; the table is memory for that reasoning.

progression.title: 1. Start with the recursive question
progression.body: For n >= 0, ways(n) asks how many ordered one-or-two-step sequences reach n. The two recursive branches share smaller questions such as ways(n−2), so a plain recursion repeats work. Its running time is exponential (O(2^n) is an upper bound) and its stack depth is O(n).

progression.title: 2. Cache repeated states
progression.body: An Integer array distinguishes an uncomputed null from a stored answer. Each n is solved once; counting constant-time integer arithmetic, this version uses O(n) time and O(n) cache plus call-stack space. These int examples are intended for n <= 45.

progression.title: 3. Fill the same states in order
progression.body: Bottom-up evaluation keeps the state definition and recurrence. It changes the order of computation: smaller stairs are complete before larger stairs read them. It uses O(n) time and O(n) table space without recursive calls.

progression.title: 4. Keep only live dependencies
progression.body: The Climbing Stairs implementation below retains only the last two counts. That reduces auxiliary space to O(1), while time remains O(n). This compression is valid because no later transition reads an older stair count; it is not a rule for every one-dimensional DP.

intuition: Grid DP applies when allowed moves create an acyclic dependency structure. With right/down movement, every arrival at a cell comes from above or left, so row-major order computes predecessors first.

A grid picture does not automatically imply DP. If moves can cycle in four directions, a plain top-left-to-bottom-right fill generally cannot finalize values; the problem may need traversal or shortest paths.
steps: Define the cell meaning
dp[r][c] may count paths to the cell or hold the minimum cost including that cell.
Classify the final move
Every non-origin path arrives from above or left, giving the recurrence.
Set origin and borders
The origin has one empty-move path for counting, but its own cell cost for minimum-sum problems.
Fill dependencies first
Row-major order works because above is in the previous row and left was just computed.
Read the destination
Then ask which earlier rows remain necessary before compressing storage.
patterns: Add predecessor counts because final moves partition paths into disjoint cases.
Take the smaller predecessor cost and add the current cell’s cost.
A blocked cell contributes zero paths; it cannot pass along a stale count.

examples.baseline: Enumerating every right/down path has combinatorial growth, and many paths repeatedly reach the same cell.
reasoning: Let dp[r][c] count paths from the origin to this cell. For an interior cell, every path ends from above or left, so add those counts.
An unobstructed first row or column has exactly one path. Fill the rest after those boundary states are known.
codeNotes: The table uses 3×3 to expose each addition; the problem card’s 3×7 example evaluates to 28.
The 2D implementation keeps every cell for clarity before considering a rolling row.
examples.takeaway: Count disjoint last-move cases; do not count the same path through multiple descriptions.

examples.baseline: Enumerating paths and summing each one repeats the same best-prefix question.
reasoning: Define dp[r][c] as the minimum path sum including grid[r][c]. Any optimal path must use an optimal path to whichever predecessor it chose.
At the origin, use the cell cost. On borders there is only one predecessor; interior cells choose the cheaper of two.
codeNotes: Separate origin and border branches avoid pretending an out-of-grid predecessor has cost zero.
This implementation allocates a new table, so the input grid stays unchanged.
examples.takeaway: Initialization depends on the meaning of a state: path count and path cost have different origins.

25.optimization: A rolling row reduces O(RC) storage to O(C): before updating dp[c], it means “above”; after updating dp[c−1], that entry means “left.” For obstacles, explicitly reset dp[c] to zero. If you need to reconstruct a path, keep predecessor choices or use an additional reconstruction strategy.
pitfalls: Initializing every border to one despite obstacles
A blocked border cell also blocks cells after it along that border.
Using zero as an impossible minimum
Zero may incorrectly win over every real positive cost.
Reading compressed entries with the wrong meaning
During a row, the array intentionally mixes previous-row and current-row values.
25.interview: “I will define what reaching a cell means and classify paths by their final move. The movement rules form a dependency order, so I can fill each state after its predecessors and then compress unused rows.”
25.summary: A grid recurrence is a last-move argument plus a valid dependency order.

intuition: Knapsack-style DP represents a resource total such as weight, amount, or sum. The state compresses many different selections that have the same remaining implications for future choices.

Before writing loops, answer two questions: can an item be reused, and does order distinguish answers? A loop direction or nesting change can silently turn “use once” into “reuse freely,” or combinations into ordered sequences.
steps: Define the resource state
Say whether dp[s] means reachable, minimum items, or number of ways to make total s.
Set the empty-selection base
Sum zero is reachable, needs zero coins, and has one empty combination.
Derive skip/take or final-item cases
A 0/1 choice reads the previous item stage; unlimited reuse may read the current stage.
Choose loop order from dependencies
With compressed 0/1 states scan sums downward. For unlimited reuse, upward scans can reuse the current item.
Interpret impossible states
Use false or an appropriate infinity sentinel, and translate failure to the requested output.
patterns: Each occurrence is available once; boolean OR combines skip and take.
Choose a final coin and minimize one plus the smaller amount’s answer.
With reusable coins, put coins outside and increasing sums inside; sum-first counting instead distinguishes order.

examples.baseline: Trying every subset explores 2^n choices even when many subsets reach the same sum.
reasoning: Equal partition is equivalent to selecting a subset totaling half the full sum. If the total is odd, no such integer target exists.
After processing an item x, reachable sums come from either skipping x or adding it to a sum possible before x. A downward scan preserves that previous-stage meaning in one array.

trace.caption: Partition [1,5,11,5], target 11
rows: Each 5 is a distinct available item

codeNotes: With x=5 and an upward scan, a newly true dp[5] could make dp[10] true using the same occurrence twice.
Only the numeric target bounds the array; O(nS) is pseudo-polynomial in input encoding size.
examples.takeaway: Loop direction expresses which version of a state a transition reads.

examples.baseline: A recursive search tries every possible final coin repeatedly; choosing the largest coin greedily fails for [1,3,4] and amount 6.
reasoning: Let dp[s] be the minimum coins for amount s. Removing the final coin c leaves amount s−c, so minimize dp[s−c]+1 across valid denominations.
Initialize dp[0]=0 and all other entries to amount+1. Positive integer coins guarantee that any feasible solution uses at most amount coins, so the sentinel is larger than every valid answer.
codeNotes: The sum-first order is valid for minimization; different orderings of the same coins do not change a minimum.
A sentinel remaining above amount means impossible and becomes -1.
examples.takeaway: Distinguish the optimization objective from the rules about reuse and ordering.

26.optimization: Start with a 2D item-by-sum table if compressed dependencies feel unclear. A 0/1 transition reads dp[i−1][s] and dp[i−1][s−x]; compression then explains the downward scan. Counting Coin Change II uses dp[0]=1, coin-first loops, and upward sums; this differs from minimum-coin initialization.
pitfalls: Scanning 0/1 sums upward
The same item can be reused within one stage.
Initializing minimum states to zero
Zero incorrectly beats every actual coin count.
Counting permutations when combinations were requested
Sum-first counting can count 1+2 and 2+1 separately.
26.interview: “My state records the answer for a resource total. I will state whether each item is reusable and derive the transition from that rule before choosing loop order. The cost depends on the numeric target as well as the item count.”
26.summary: The loops encode the selection rules; derive them from the uncompressed state meaning.

intuition: Two-sequence DP compares prefixes. A pair of prefix lengths captures exactly how much of each input has been considered, letting many different match or edit histories share one state.

A subsequence may skip positions while preserving order; a substring must be contiguous. That single distinction changes the recurrence. For subsequences, a mismatch often means skipping a character rather than resetting progress.
steps: Define prefix lengths
dp[i][j] refers to the first i and first j characters; their final characters are at i−1 and j−1.
Classify the final characters
Separate matching and mismatching cases and enumerate every legal final action.
Initialize empty prefixes
LCS with an empty string is zero; editing to or from an empty string costs the other length.
Fill predecessor states first
Left, above, and diagonal values must be ready before computing the current entry.
Separate length from reconstruction
A scalar optimum does not automatically provide the actual sequence or edit script.
patterns: A match extends a diagonal; a mismatch drops one final character.
Insert, delete, and replace correspond to three predecessor states.
LIS dp[i] means the best subsequence ending exactly at i, and the final answer is max(dp), not necessarily its last entry.

examples.baseline: Enumerating subsequences and checking each against the other string requires exponential work.
reasoning: If final characters match, they can extend an optimal LCS of the shorter prefixes. If they differ, at least one is omitted, so take the better of dropping either one.
The leading zero row and column express empty-prefix answers and remove special cases from the recurrence.

trace.caption: LCS of abc and ac; columns are prefixes of ac

codeNotes: The table uses abc/ac for a compact trace; abcde/ace in the problem card follows the same recurrence and returns 3.
On mismatch, retain the best neighboring prefix result; resetting to zero would describe a different contiguous-match problem.
examples.takeaway: Dropping a final character explores an alternative without discarding earlier valid matches.

examples.baseline: Recursively trying insert, delete, and replace revisits the same pair of remaining prefixes.
reasoning: Let dp[i][j] be the minimum edits from a[0:i] to b[0:j]. A deletion comes from dp[i−1][j], an insertion from dp[i][j−1], and a replacement from dp[i−1][j−1].
Matching final characters cost no edit and use the diagonal directly. Empty-prefix borders count the necessary insertions or deletions.

trace.caption: Edit distance from horse to ros

codeNotes: The three operations add one only when the final characters differ.
One optimal script is horse → rorse → rose → ros, using replacement, deletion, deletion.
examples.takeaway: Each transition should name a concrete final operation on the represented prefixes.

27.optimization: A rolling row reduces length-only LCS or edit-distance memory, but preserve the old diagonal before overwriting it. For LIS, minimal tails plus binary search improves O(n²) to O(n log n); the tails array itself is not necessarily a subsequence. Reconstruction needs additional choices or predecessor indices.
pitfalls: Confusing an index with a prefix length
dp[i][j] compares characters at i−1 and j−1.
Using zero edit-distance borders
Transforming a nonempty prefix to empty requires deletions.
Returning only the final LIS endpoint
The longest subsequence can end before the final input element.
27.interview: “A state represents two prefixes. I will classify their final characters, map each permitted action to a smaller prefix pair, and use empty prefixes as the base cases. Then I will distinguish computing the optimum from reconstructing it.”
27.summary: Turn a comparison of whole sequences into decisions about their final characters.

intuition: A greedy algorithm commits to a choice without revisiting alternatives. It is correct only when a proof shows that commitment cannot make the best achievable result worse.

Two useful proofs are exchange and dominance. Exchange replaces a choice in an optimal solution with your greedy choice. Dominance shows that one retained summary is at least as useful as every discarded alternative.
steps: State the local choice
Say exactly what you keep or select: earliest finish, lowest price so far, or farthest reachable boundary.
Compare against an alternative
Explain why a solution using a different first choice can be changed without harm.
Preserve the remaining problem
After committing, verify that the same argument applies to what remains.
Search for counterexamples
Test the rule against cases where an attractive immediate choice blocks future progress.
patterns: Keep the largest reachable prefix boundary when smaller reaches offer no additional possibilities.
For maximum compatible interval count, finish as early as possible to leave room.
For one stock transaction, retain the minimum earlier price when evaluating a sale today.

examples.baseline: Trying every legal jump can explore many paths; DP could store reachability for every index.
reasoning: Because every jump length up to nums[i] is allowed, reachable positions form a prefix. A single farthest boundary summarizes that prefix.
Only reachable indices can extend farthest. If i exceeds it, no earlier reachable position can cross the gap, so the destination is impossible.
codeNotes: Check i > farthest before using nums[i]. An unreachable index must not extend the range.
The method keeps a reachable set summary; it does not construct the sequence of jumps.
examples.takeaway: Greedy can retain a dominant summary rather than literally choose one jump.

examples.baseline: Enumerating subsets of intervals and testing compatibility is exponential.
reasoning: Minimizing removals is equivalent to maximizing the number kept. Sort by finishing time and keep the next compatible interval.

Replace the first interval of an optimal compatible schedule with the earliest-finishing available one. It ends no later, so every later interval in that schedule remains compatible. Repeat on the remaining suffix.
codeNotes: The two end-3 intervals may appear in either tie order; the final count is unchanged.
Touching is allowed, so only start < end is rejected.
examples.takeaway: The exchange proof explains why earliest finish, rather than earliest start, is the useful order.

28.optimization: A correct greedy summary often removes a DP dimension, but only after a dominance proof. Coin denominations [1,3,4] and amount 6 refute “take the largest coin first”: 4+1+1 loses to 3+3. Count sorting workspace separately from the constant state of a greedy scan.
pitfalls: Mistaking a plausible rule for a proof
Several successful examples do not establish optimality.
Sorting intervals by start for scheduling
A very early long interval can block many short ones.
Discarding useful state too soon
If two histories offer different future options, one scalar may not dominate both.
28.interview: “I will justify this choice with an exchange argument: replacing an optimal solution’s first choice with mine leaves at least as much room for the rest. Then I can repeat the argument on the remaining instance.”
28.summary: Commit only after proving the alternatives cannot improve the future.

intuition: A trie shares storage for common prefixes. Each edge consumes one character, and the node reached after reading a prefix represents all stored words that begin with it.

Reaching a node does not imply a complete word ends there. A terminal marker distinguishes “this prefix exists” from “this exact word was inserted.” That distinction is central to both exact search and wildcard search.
steps: Choose the alphabet representation
An array of 26 children fits lowercase English letters; other alphabets may call for maps.
Walk one character per edge
Create missing nodes during insertion; reject missing edges during exact lookup.
Mark complete words
Set an end flag only after every character has been consumed.
Branch only when required
A wildcard consumes exactly one character and tries each existing child.
Interpret the final node
Prefix queries require existence; word queries also require the terminal marker.
patterns: Share the same walk but check different completion conditions.
Combine trie navigation with backtracking over existing child edges.
Stop at the first terminal prefix when replacing words with their shortest root.

examples.baseline: A set supports exact membership, but testing a prefix by scanning every stored word repeats character work.
reasoning: Insertion follows or creates one node per character. Common beginnings reuse the same path, so inserting app after apple shares its first three edges.
search requires the reached node to be terminal; startsWith only requires the path to exist.
codeNotes: c − a maps lowercase English characters to child slots; it is not a general Unicode mapping.
The root also represents the empty prefix, though the original problem restricts word lengths.
examples.takeaway: A path represents a prefix; a terminal flag represents membership as a complete word.

examples.baseline: Scanning every stored word for every wildcard query costs time proportional to the entire dictionary.
reasoning: A recursive search state is a trie node plus the next pattern index. A letter chooses one edge; a dot tries all existing children.
Success requires consuming the entire pattern at a terminal node. A dot matches one character, not an arbitrary-length substring.

trace.caption: Dictionary {bad,dad,mad}, pattern .ad
rows: Any one terminal match gives true

codeNotes: The implementation short-circuits after one successful branch, so it may not visit every branch shown.
The recursive base case checks node.end rather than returning true solely because the pattern ended.
examples.takeaway: Wildcards change a single path lookup into a search over matching prefixes.

29.optimization: Exact operations take O(L) time for length L. Wildcards can branch widely and are not generally O(L). An array of children trades constant-time access for many empty slots; sparse maps can reduce those slots at different overhead. charAt loops avoid the temporary arrays used by toCharArray.
pitfalls: Treating every prefix as a word
search(app) must stay false after inserting only apple.
Claiming wildcard lookup is always linear
Several dots can explore many trie nodes.
Using a fixed 26-letter index for other input
Validate or change the child representation when the alphabet changes.
29.interview: “Each node represents a prefix, and a terminal flag marks complete words. Exact characters choose one child; a wildcard branches over existing children while advancing one pattern position.”
29.summary: Organize words by shared beginnings, and keep prefix existence separate from complete-word membership.

intuition: Bit operations act independently on fixed-width binary positions. They are useful when the problem’s structure matches an algebraic identity, such as equal values canceling under XOR.

Start by writing the identity and its assumptions. XOR removes pairs, not arbitrary duplicates; clearing one set bit counts bits, not numeric decrements. Java int has 32 bits, which also shapes overflow and shift behavior.
steps: State the bit identity
For XOR: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. For clearing a bit: n & (n−1) removes the lowest set bit.
Match it to the input guarantee
Pair cancellation requires exactly paired duplicates except for the target value.
Choose a neutral initial value
XOR accumulation starts at zero.
Define termination for signed values
Use n != 0 when counting all set bits in an int bit pattern.
State the width model
At most 32 iterations is constant time for Java int, though a variable-width model may use O(b).
patterns: Combine all values when unwanted contributions occur in equal pairs.
Repeatedly clear the lowest set bit to count or iterate set positions.
Counting Bits uses a smaller number’s answer plus the current low bit, or the answer after clearing one bit.

examples.baseline: A frequency map uses O(n) extra memory; sorting needs extra work or changes input order.
reasoning: XOR is associative and commutative, so equal values can be grouped conceptually even when they appear far apart.
Each pair becomes zero, and zero does not change the remaining value. The guarantee that exactly one value is unpaired makes the final accumulator the answer.
codeNotes: Intermediate values need not be input values; only the cancellation identity matters.
The same identity works for negative int bit patterns.
examples.takeaway: The input multiplicity guarantee is part of the correctness proof.

examples.baseline: Testing all 32 bit positions is already constant time; clearing set bits visits only positions containing one.
reasoning: Subtracting one flips the lowest one to zero and all trailing zeros to ones. AND with the original value keeps higher bits but removes that lowest one.
Each iteration removes exactly one set bit, so the iteration count is the answer.

trace.caption: Count bits of 11, shown in four binary positions

codeNotes: n != 0 handles signed patterns as well as positive integers.
Even when n is the int sign-bit pattern, Java’s fixed-width subtraction and AND still clear one set bit.
examples.takeaway: Count a monotone structural change: exactly one one-bit disappears per step.

30.optimization: For fixed-width int, a full bit scan is also O(1); the set-bit loop is O(b) for b set bits and at most 32. Use >>> for zero-fill right shifts when required, and remember Java masks int shift distances to five bits, so 1 << 32 is not a new 33rd bit.
pitfalls: Applying XOR to triple duplicates
Three equal values leave one copy rather than canceling.
Using n > 0 to count all bits
Negative signed representations would be skipped.
Confusing & and &&
One combines bit patterns; the other combines boolean conditions with short-circuiting.
30.interview: “I will state the identity and show how the input guarantee lets unwanted values cancel. For bit counting, each iteration clears exactly one set bit, so both correctness and the iteration bound follow.”
30.summary: A bit trick is an algebraic proof applied to a fixed-width representation.
